opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I think I got pretty lucky with the timing more than anything else. When I started my PhD at Recital, which was a startup, in partnership with Sorbonne, the field was in this interesting transitional moment. I chose to work on natural language generation, and at the time, people around me were a bit skeptical. The common wisdom was that generation was kind of the "hard, messy" side of NLP: evaluation was unreliable, outputs were often incoherent, and a lot of the industry value seemed to be in classification, extraction, understanding tasks.

But I had this intuition that generation was where things would eventually converge. If you can generate well, you can in principle solve almost any task, because you can frame everything as producing text. So I spent a lot of my PhD on things like summarization, question generation, and especially evaluation of generated text, because I felt that if we couldn't measure quality properly, we couldn't make progress. Some of that work, like using question answering to evaluate summaries for factual consistency, was really about trying to get beyond n-gram overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE, which were clearly breaking down as models got better.

I also worked on reinforcement learning applied to language generation, things like GANs for text and RL-based fine-tuning. At the time it was quite niche, and frankly a lot of it didn't work that well. But it gave me a feel for the problem of optimizing a language model toward some reward signal rather than just imitating data. And of course, a few years later, that became central with RLHF.

So my honest assessment is that the topic choice was good, partly by conviction and partly by luck. The conviction was that generation and learning from feedback would matter. The luck was that scaling arrived right at the moment when those ideas became practical. If I'd finished my PhD five years earlier, a lot of what I did would have stayed academic curiosities. Instead, it ended up being directly relevant to what I worked on afterwards, on Galactica, on Llama, and on the post-training side of large language models.

If I have one piece of advice from that experience, it's: pick a topic you believe will matter in five years, even if it looks unfashionable or impractical today. The things that seem a bit crazy are often where the leverage is.

r001.rationale: He says he got lucky with the timing “more than anything else” and describes the choice as partly luck, while presenting conviction as only part of the explanation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, honestly, I think it was a pretty good choice, though some of it was luck and some of it was conviction.

When I started around 2018, I was doing a CIFRE PhD, which in France means you're split between a company, Recital, and a lab, LIP6 at Sorbonne. The topic was natural language generation, specifically summarization and how to evaluate it. And at the time, generation was not the hot thing. Everyone was working on classification, on BERT-style understanding tasks. Generation was considered hard, messy, kind of a niche. People would ask me, why summarization? Nobody can even evaluate it properly.

And that was exactly the point for me. I felt that generation was the general form of the problem. If you can generate text, you can in principle do any task by framing it as generation. And the evaluation question was the bottleneck. ROUGE and BLEU were clearly broken, and I thought if we don't fix how we measure, we can't make progress. So a lot of my thesis was about learned metrics, question-based evaluation like QuestEval, and also using reinforcement learning to optimize generation beyond maximum likelihood, which was quite unpopular then.

In hindsight, that bet aged well. Generation became the whole field with GPT-3 and after. Evaluation became one of the hardest open problems, and RL for language models became central. So the themes I picked turned out to be the right ones, and that experience is a big part of why I ended up working on things like Galactica, Toolformer, and then Llama 2 at Meta, where RLHF and evaluation were at the core.

The part I'd criticize is that I was maybe too close to the academic framing. I spent a lot of time on specific benchmarks and clever metric design when the real lesson, which I only fully absorbed later, was about scale and data. But I don't regret it. Doing the PhD in an industrial setting taught me to care about things actually working, not just publishing, and that mindset mattered more than any single paper.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the choice as partly luck but also as conviction based on a deliberate view of generation and evaluation; it does not characterize the choice as chance rather than foresight.

astra-6.text: I think a good PhD topic gives you a direction without locking you into one particular solution. You want a question that matters, but also room to discover that your initial assumptions were wrong. That’s how I would assess the choice: did it help me develop research taste, ask better questions, and become more independent? The specific topic is part of it, but learning how to do research is the more lasting outcome.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates the topic by whether it offered direction, room to explore, and lasting research skills. It does not characterize the choice as chance rather than visionary foresight.

sol-6.1.text: I’d assess it less by whether the exact topic is still fashionable and more by whether it taught me how to do research. Can you identify an important problem, question your assumptions, and learn something when an experiment fails? Working between a company and a university also means asking both whether an idea is scientifically interesting and whether it’s useful. That’s the balance I would look for in judging the choice.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates the topic by what it taught him and its scientific and practical value; it does not describe the choice as chance rather than foresight.
